doc.title: Artie Shaw — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Breakup, the 1940 band and the Navy
title: The Navy band measured against the Musicraft band; A Mixed Bag and the Meltones
summary: Shaw rates the Navy band below the Musicraft band, says he regained those masters and will issue them, and praises Kitty Kallen and Mel Torme's Meltones.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: It was a real all-star band in many ways.
Well, yeah. I didn’t think of it that way. I just got good guys that could play. We had a good book.
How do you think it measured up in comparison to your other bands, the bands that had come before it?

If I’d had time to take that band and whip it into the kind of shape I did, it could have made some good records. It would have been comparable to . . . not quite as good as the Musicraft band with Roy Eldridge. That kind of band. That kind of book. By the way, I’m going to release those records. I finally got the rights to them. I sued Musicraft. I got all the . . . the copyrights have reverted to me. I’m putting out an album
called A Mixed Bag. Did you ever hear the Kitty Kallen record of My Heart Belongs To Daddy? I’ll play it for you, if you want to hear it.
We don’t want to put it on this, because . . . But it’s an amazing record. A vocal record. And Mel Tormé and the Meltones. Did you ever hear some of the records we did?
Like What Is This Thing Called Love. Nobody’s ever used a quartet like that, or a singing group. They were part of the band. Mel still remembers that with great fondness.
[A sudden change of topic; perhaps a change of tape?]
